candidates.text:
The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

Moderator: Same opening this week, several continuations, names removed. The opening is: In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance. Here they are.

A. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

D. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

They were silver fish then, bright as minnows, with lantern hearts, and the sea glowed from shore to shore so that no creature of the Deep ever knew darkness. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, curious as children and careless as only bright things can be.
